day_context.tournament_summary: The last dance gets a quarter-final. Belgium's golden generation — De Bruyne, Lukaku, Courtois, the group that finished third in 2018 and has never won a thing — arrives at SoFi Stadium with the tournament down to eight, and across from it stands the opposite of itself: a Spain side already holding the 2010 World Cup and the 2024 European title, now rebuilt around teenagers. It is also, quietly, a rematch four decades in the making. The last time these two met with a World Cup semi-final on the line, in Puebla in 1986, Belgium won a shootout by scoring all five — the first team in World Cup history to do it — and marched to the best finish in their history. Tonight the country that keeps making great teams that fall just short tries once more, against the country that keeps finding a way to finish the job.
context_notes: Spain vs Belgium at SoFi Stadium, Los Angeles — World Cup quarter-final. Their third World Cup meeting: Belgium won the 1986 quarter-final on penalties, Spain won 2-1 in the 1990 group stage — one decisive result each, with tonight the decider.

The 1986 quarter-final in Puebla ended 1-1 after extra time (Ceulemans for Belgium, Señor equalising late for Spain) and Belgium won the shootout 5-4 — the first side in World Cup history to convert all five penalties. They reached the semi-finals, still bettered only by their third place in 2018.

Belgium's 'golden generation' — Kevin De Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku, Thibaut Courtois — peaked at third at the 2018 World Cup and has never won a major trophy; this is widely framed as its final World Cup. Eden Hazard, the fourth name of that era, retired in 2023.

Spain arrive as reigning European champions (Euro 2024, beating England 2-1 in the final) and 2010 world champions, now rebuilt around a teenage core — Lamine Yamal, 18, and Pedri — the youngest spine of any side left in the tournament.
Belgium reached the quarter-final by beating the host United States 4-1 in the Round of 16; Spain edged Portugal 1-0.

here_there_thread.topic: The two ends of a golden generation
here_there_thread.framing: Belgium is the country that keeps building great teams and keeps not quite winning. Forty years ago a side of Pfaff, Scifo and Ceulemans reached a World Cup semi-final on a flawless penalty shootout against Spain — and then lost to Maradona. A generation later the most gifted group Belgium has ever produced — De Bruyne, Lukaku, Hazard, Courtois — finished third in 2018, sat top of the world rankings for years, and retired one by one without a single trophy between them. Tonight what's left of that group, De Bruyne at 35 and Lukaku at 33, plays what everyone accepts is its last World Cup. And the team across from it is the argument against everything Belgium has lived: Spain, who won the World Cup at their first golden-generation peak in 2010, won Europe again in 2024, and have already handed the keys to an 18-year-old. One side is trying to finish a twenty-year story before the final whistle of a career. The other has a teenager who thinks the story is just starting. The thread runs from Puebla to Los Angeles — the country that falls just short, meeting the country that doesn't.

facts.label: Puebla, 1986
facts.fact: Belgium's first golden generation reached the 1986 World Cup semi-finals by beating Spain in a quarter-final shootout — converting all five penalties, the first team in World Cup history to do so — the deepest run in Belgian history until 2018.

facts.label: The trophy that never came
facts.fact: The De Bruyne–Lukaku–Hazard–Courtois generation topped the world rankings for a record stretch and finished third at the 2018 World Cup, but won no major tournament; Hazard retired in 2023, and 2026 is widely seen as the last World Cup for De Bruyne (35) and Lukaku (33).

facts.label: Spain, both ends of the arc
facts.fact: Spain won the 2010 World Cup with their own golden generation and were European champions again at Euro 2024 — and have already rebuilt around Lamine Yamal, who was 17 when he starred at that Euro, the youngest player ever to appear in a European Championship final.

facts.label: Los Angeles, tonight
facts.fact: At SoFi Stadium the two collide again with a semi-final at stake — Belgium chasing the one prize its greatest players never won, Spain carrying a teenager who has barely started counting.

story_behind_number.historical_anchor: Forty years ago, almost to the week, Spain and Belgium played a World Cup quarter-final in the heat of Puebla, Mexico, and it went the distance. Jan Ceulemans put Belgium ahead just after the half-hour; Spain's substitute Señor forced it level with five minutes left; extra time settled nothing. So it went to penalties — and Belgium made history the hard way, scoring all five, the first team ever to complete a perfect five-from-five shootout at a World Cup. Spain's only miss, from Eloy, was saved by Jean-Marie Pfaff, and Belgium marched on to a semi-final and the best World Cup finish they would have for the next thirty-two years. Forty is the gap between that afternoon and this one — long enough that not one player from Puebla is anywhere near tonight's teams, long enough that Belgium has since built and buried a second, even more gifted golden generation, and long enough to make a quarter-final between the same two nations feel less like coincidence than a debt being called in.

supporting_context: The 1986 quarter-final was played at Estadio Cuauhtémoc in Puebla; Belgium went on to lose the semi-final to Diego Maradona's Argentina, the eventual champions.
Belgium reached that shootout with the closest thing the country had to a golden generation before the current one — Jean-Marie Pfaff in goal, a young Enzo Scifo, the captain Jan Ceulemans.

Since 1986 the two have met once more at a World Cup, in the 1990 group stage, where Spain won 2-1 — which is why, whatever the modern form guide says, tonight reads as a rubber match four decades in the writing.

narrative_beats: Mexico 1986, a quarter-final in the thin, hot air of Puebla: Spain, built around the elegant Emilio Butragueño, against a Belgium side that had crept out of its group and was quietly becoming the best team the country had ever sent to a World Cup.

Jan Ceulemans, the captain, put Belgium ahead just after the half-hour, and for the better part of an hour it looked like enough — until the substitute Señor lashed in an equaliser with five minutes left and dragged the tie through 90 minutes and a scoreless extra time to penalties.

Then Belgium did something no team had done at a World Cup before: they scored all five. Claesen, Scifo, Broos, Vervoort, Van der Elst — five from five, the first flawless shootout in the tournament's history. Spain's only miss, Eloy's, was pushed away by Jean-Marie Pfaff, and it was over, 5-4.

Belgium went on to the semi-final and a defeat to Maradona's Argentina, but the run stood as the high-water mark of Belgian football for thirty-two years — until a second, even more celebrated generation matched it with third place in 2018. Forty years on, the same two nations meet at the same stage, and Belgium's current group, running out of tournaments, would take Puebla's ending gladly.

back_story.ledger: Two World Cup meetings, one decisive result each. Belgium won the 1986 quarter-final on penalties — 1-1 after extra time, then a perfect 5-4 shootout, the first five-from-five in World Cup history — and reached the semi-finals. Spain answered in the 1990 group stage, winning 2-1. That leaves the head-to-head level at a World Cup, and tonight in Los Angeles the same fixture returns at the very round it turned on four decades ago, with a semi-final and — for Belgium's fading golden generation — very likely a last chance on the line.

from_the_stands.question: I've followed this Belgium team through every near-miss and I'm almost afraid to hope. Has this golden generation actually ever won anything, and have we ever beaten Spain when it mattered? I keep hearing about 1986 but that was before I was born.

facts: The current golden generation — De Bruyne, Lukaku, Courtois, and the retired Hazard — has never won a major trophy. Its high point is third place at the 2018 World Cup, Belgium's best-ever finish; it was also ranked world number one for a record stretch without silverware to show for it.

Belgium have beaten Spain when it mattered, but you have to go back to 1986: a World Cup quarter-final in Puebla, 1-1 after extra time, won 5-4 on penalties — and it remains one of only two times Belgium has ever reached a World Cup semi-final.
The teams have met once more at a World Cup since, the 1990 group stage, and Spain won that one 2-1 — so the World Cup head-to-head is level.

Spain arrive as the reigning European champions (Euro 2024) and 2010 world champions, rebuilt around 18-year-old Lamine Yamal — the toughest possible test for a Belgian side trying to finally turn its talent into a trophy.
factual_brief.note: The fear is earned — this is a group that has spent a decade being the best team never to win — but the history isn't all heartbreak. Belgium have beaten Spain on the World Cup's biggest afternoon before, in that 1986 shootout Dieter is too young to remember, and it carried them to the semi-finals. What tonight really asks is whether the same fixture, at the same stage, can rescue a generation that is almost out of chances. Spain are the hardest imaginable opponent for it — young, decorated, unbothered — which is exactly why beating them would mean everything.
